Healthcare. Gasoline. Electricity. Mortgage rates. Water bills. Up. Up. Up. Up. Up. The cost of basic goods and services – now a leading issue in the midterm elections – continues to rise and Americans are feeling pinched. But as the midterms approach and lame-duck sessions follow, advocates are already preparing to make their case to a fresh bundle of lawmakers. Neither in Lansing nor on Capitol Hill has water affordability legislation gained enough support to become law. It does not appear likely that any action will take place before new members are sworn into office next year. Sign up “We’re really looking towards January and a new administration and a new majority legislature that will allow us to be able to move on some important bills,” said Sylvia Orduño, who has been on the frontlines of the debate as an organizer for the Michigan Welfare Rights Organization. It can hardly wait that long. About half of lower income households surveyed by Pew Research in July and August said they could not pay all their monthly bills on time. Pew did not ask directly about water bills, but pressure there is mounting. Wayne Metro Community Action Agency runs a state-funded program to assist low-income households in the greater Detroit area who have fallen behind on their water payments. A new application window for assistance opens each week, said Melissa Davis, who directs the program.
